meeting-wrapup.title: Wrap up meeting notes
meeting-wrapup.description: Turns meeting notes into decisions, action items with owners and due dates, and open questions.
meeting-wrapup.markdown:
Use this on meeting notes: the page the person names, or notes they paste.

## Steps

1. Read all of the notes before writing anything.
2. Find every decision. A decision is something the meeting agreed on, not something it only discussed.
3. Find every action item: what has to be done, who does it and by when. Take names and dates only from the notes; where one is missing, write "not set" instead of guessing.
4. Find the questions left open and the topics put off to another meeting.

## Answer

- **Summary:** two or three sentences on what the meeting was about and where it ended.
- **Decisions:** a list, one decision per item.
- **Action items:** a table with the columns Task, Owner and Due.
- **Open questions:** a list; leave this part out when there are none.

Keep the wording of the notes where it is clear. Don't add decisions or tasks the notes don't contain. When the person asks, add the action items as rows of the task database they name.

status-summary.title: Weekly status summary
status-summary.description: Summarizes a database of work for a period: what was finished, what is late and what is waiting, with the people involved.
status-summary.markdown:
Use this on a database of work (tasks, projects, jobs, orders) the person names. Unless they say otherwise, the period is the last seven days.

## Steps

1. Look at the database's properties: which one says whether the work is done (a status), which one is the due date and which one is the owner.
2. Find the rows finished in the period (done, and changed in the period when there is no completion date), the rows past their due date that aren't done, and the rows marked as waiting or blocked.
3. Count each group.

## Answer

- **In short:** one sentence with the counts, for example "12 finished, 3 late, 2 waiting".
- **Finished:** the rows finished in the period, with their owners.
- **Late:** each late row with its due date and owner, the longest overdue first.
- **Waiting:** each waiting or blocked row, with what it waits for when the row says so.

Name every row as it is titled in the database. When the database has no status or due date, say which part of the summary that leaves out instead of guessing.

customer-reply.title: Reply to a customer
customer-reply.description: Drafts a clear, polite reply to a customer's message, using only what the workspace says about the customer and the subject.
customer-reply.markdown:
Use this when the person shares a customer's message (pasted, or on a page) and wants a reply drafted.

## Steps

1. Work out what the customer asks for or complains about, and what they expect to happen next.
2. Look in the workspace for what is known about this customer and subject: their page or row, earlier offers, orders and notes. Use only what you find; never promise prices, dates or terms the workspace doesn't state.
3. Where the reply needs a fact you couldn't find, leave a placeholder in square brackets, like [delivery date], and list the placeholders after the draft.

## Draft

- Start with a subject line.
- Write in the customer's language, as formally as they wrote.
- Open with the answer or the next step, not with long thanks or apologies.
- Use short paragraphs, and a list when there are several steps or items.
- End with what happens next and who does it.

Write only the draft; don't send anything.

proofread.title: Proofread a text
proofread.description: Checks a page or a pasted text for spelling, grammar, unclear sentences and tone, and suggests each fix with the reason for it.
proofread.markdown:
Use this on a page or a text the person pastes, before it goes to a customer, a colleague or the public.

## What to check

1. Spelling, grammar and punctuation.
2. Sentences that can be read in two ways, or that are too long to follow.
3. Numbers, dates, names and amounts that contradict each other within the text.
4. Tone: whether it suits the people who will read it. Ask who they are only when the text doesn't make it clear.

## Answer

- A table with the columns Original, Suggestion and Why, in the order the problems appear in the text.
- After it, at most three remarks about the text as a whole.
- When there is nothing to fix, say so in one sentence.

Keep the author's voice: suggest only what fixes a problem, not rewording to your taste. Change the page itself only when the person asks.

triage-request.title: Triage a request
triage-request.description: Reads an incoming request or complaint and proposes its subject, priority and who should handle it, with a short reason.
triage-request.markdown:
Use this on a request, complaint or support message: a database row, a page, or a text the person pastes.

## Steps

1. Say in one sentence what the request is about.
2. Decide the priority:
   - **Urgent:** something is stopped or unsafe, or a customer is losing money or time right now.
   - **High:** a firm deadline in the next few days, or an important customer waiting.
   - **Normal:** anything else that needs an answer.
   - **Low:** questions and wishes with no deadline.
3. Propose who should handle it. When the request is a row of a database with options for its subject, priority or owner, choose from those options; otherwise look in the workspace for who handled similar requests.
4. Note what is missing to act on it, like an order number or an address.

## Answer

A short list: Subject, Priority, Handled by and Missing, then one sentence on why it has that priority. When the person asks, set these on the row.

executive-summary.title: Executive summary
executive-summary.description: Condenses a long page into five points for a busy reader: what it is about, what was decided and what is needed from them.
executive-summary.markdown:
Use this on a long page: a report, a proposal, a plan or a long thread of notes.

## Steps

1. Read the whole page, its tables included.
2. Pick what a busy reader must know: the purpose, the main facts and figures, the decisions and the risks.
3. Find what the page needs from the reader: an approval, a choice, a date.

## Answer

- A first line saying what the page is, in at most ten words.
- At most five points, the most important first, one sentence each. Keep figures, dates and names exactly as the page has them.
- **Needed from you:** the decision or action the page asks for, or "nothing".

Leave out background and detail the reader doesn't need to act. Don't add opinions, or facts that aren't on the page.
